parsed.explanation: The operative regime is the parent nation's, applied locally with no local override: no criminalisation of trans identity or same-sex relations, gender-identity anti-discrimination in force since 2012, transphobia an aggravating circumstance since 2017, conversion therapy banned, marriage recognised, and marker change without surgery since 2017. Those are real, documented protections that a visitor inherits. Against them: a documented pattern — not a single anecdote — of trans women with a male legal marker placed in all-male custody, with the national preventive mechanism finding persistent serious violations across roughly 40 trans detainees since 2010 and no remediation. Care is uneven and locally absent. Social acceptance is constrained by religious and customary norms, with no local evidence of the protections actually being enforced. Custody placement is the harshest operative feature and the reason this sits below the acceptance-with-working-remedies tier.

entry_documents.exposure: No documented border or airport screening practice specific to trans travellers; no non-binary/X marker is obtainable under parent law, so an X-marker passport is an unresolved edge case.
entry_documents.protection: Parent framework applies at entry; no provision criminalises transgender people or same-sex relations; documents issued abroad are the traveller's own.
entry_documents.interaction: No documented border-actor friction, so entry risk rests on unanswered questions rather than a known exposure.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Documented: trans women whose legal gender is recorded male are held in all-male establishments (a legal grey area, one 2014 transfer to a men's facility); the national preventive mechanism's 2021 opinion, extending 2010, found persistent serious fundamental-rights violations, drawing on ~40 trans detainees since 2010.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Detention governed by parent framework with an operating preventive mechanism and formal complaint channels; transphobia is an aggravating factor for crimes.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Oversight has recorded the same violations for over a decade without remedying placement practice — corroboration of an unremedied exposure, not mitigation.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Custodial and detention facility placement is by recorded legal sex rather than lived gender; no other state facility rule (wards, shelters, changing rooms) is documented locally.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Parent anti-discrimination statute covers access to services; no local measure overriding it was identified.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Facility exposure arises only on entry into state custody, but then follows the detainee as an institutional act, not a discretionary one.

care_services.exposure: No local specialist gender-affirming care; residents travel outward; a 2022 regional report found extended waits, lack of self-determination and location-dependent inequity; a medical academy framing of demand as 'epidemic-like' signals institutional reluctance.
care_services.protection: Gender-affirming surgery lawful domestically since 1979; transsexualism funded as a long-term illness under national insurance; conversion therapy criminalised since 2022.
care_services.interaction: Funding and legality are resident-facing; a visitor needing continuity of medication faces practical scarcity rather than legal prohibition.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: No state threat-framing of trans people. A 2024 bill banning under-18 medical transition passed the upper house but has been stalled since July 2024 and is opposed by the government; its local application is unresolved.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Gender-identity discrimination prohibited in employment, housing and services since 2012; labour code bars discriminatory recruitment and dismissal measures; transphobia an aggravating circumstance; conversion therapy punishable by two years and a 30,000 euro fine.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: The protective statute is in force and reaches the territory; enforcement practice locally is not documented in either direction.

minors_guardians.exposure: A stalled national bill would bar medical transition under 18; no local specialist paediatric care exists, so a travelling family faces infrastructural gaps and unresolved legal direction rather than an operative ban.
minors_guardians.protection: No ban is currently in force; late-2024 paediatric endocrinology guidance endorses puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2.
minors_guardians.interaction: A guardian travelling with a trans minor would find no local services and unclear future direction; the operative rule today imposes no restriction.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Small, isolated population with dominant religious and local cultural norms; gender-variant customary roles coexist with stigma and concealment; no local hate-crime figures are sourced.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Transphobia as an aggravating circumstance applies framework-wide; a functioning civil society and oversight bodies exist at parent level.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Local enforcement of the hate-crime and discrimination provisions is not documented, so the paper protection is untested where the traveller actually is.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Successive preventive-mechanism opinions (2010, extended 2021) record the same custody violations without remedy; local enforcement of anti-discrimination and hate-crime law is undocumented.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Court-based marker change, statutory anti-discrimination, aggravated sentencing and a criminal conversion-therapy offence all exist and are in force.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies are documented as available but not documented as working for the specific local exposures, so they do not offset the custody placement practice.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.55-C has ward placement by document sex with denial of non-urgent care but no custodial abuse. This jurisdiction has a stronger protective statute (aggravated sentencing, in-force anti-discrimination) and no criminalisation, yet a documented custody-placement harm pattern; it sits modestly above 0.55-C because the everyday visitor exposure is legal-protected rather than administratively refused.

0.65-A involves documented friction corrected by working remedy (apology, compensation, courts ordering release). Here the counterpart exposure — birth-sex custody placement — has produced repeated oversight findings without remediation, so it falls below 0.65-A despite comparable formal protections.

0.75-C has trained border officers, brief detention, counsel access and compensation for unlawful holding. This jurisdiction documents no border practice at all and documents a harmful custody-placement rule with a decade of unremedied findings, placing it clearly below 0.75-C.

parsed.synthesis: A visitor inherits a genuinely protective parent regime: no criminalisation, enforced anti-discrimination, aggravated sentencing for transphobic crime, recognised relationships and a conversion-therapy offence. Everyday exposure — hotels, transport, shops — has no documented adverse practice, and social stigma in a tiny religiously conservative community reads as friction and concealment rather than organised hostility. The decisive negative is institutional: custody placement by recorded legal sex, with the preventive mechanism recording persistent violations against roughly 40 trans detainees since 2010 and no remedy across two opinions. That is a state-imposed, universal-exposure practice with a documented harm pattern, weighing heavily against an otherwise accommodating legal climate. Criminalisation is absent, so the extremes of the ladder do not apply; care scarcity and untested local enforcement hold it below the working-remedy tier.
